Here are the verse-by-verse research notes for Isaiah 30. I have drawn on the pages I could access. Some traditions and sites could not be reached within the search and fetch limits; I have noted what was found and what was not.

---

## ISAIAH 30 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1: *“Woe to the rebellious children,” declares the LORD, “to those who carry out a plan that is not Mine, who form an alliance, but against My will, heaping up sin upon sin.”*

- **Traditional reading:** The “woe” (or “alas”) expresses sorrow as much as indignation — the prophet has learned that Hezekiah’s court has sent an embassy to Egypt. “Take counsel, but not of Me” means the leaders consulted one another and foreign diplomats but did not consult the Lord through His word, prophets, or the Urim and Thummim. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)
- The phrase translated “form an alliance” (BSB) is literally “weave a web” or “pour out a drink-offering” — either picture describes the intricate diplomacy of treaty-making. Either rendering points to double-dealing diplomacy carried out without the Spirit’s guidance. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- “Heaping up sin upon sin”: The original sin is rejecting God’s counsel; the added sin is then trusting in a human substitute (Egypt). Guzik notes that it is one sin to reject the Lord and another sin altogether to trust in something else. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- **Gill (Reformed Baptist)** adds that this verse pictures spiritually unregenerate people who consult “flesh and blood, carnal sense and reason” instead of the gospel, covering themselves “with the rags of their own righteousness, and not with the robe of Christ’s righteousness.” (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 2: *“They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice, to seek shelter under Pharaoh’s protection and take refuge in Egypt’s shade.”*

- Judah’s leaders “walked to go down into Egypt” — meaning they sent messengers to form an alliance and secure military assistance against Assyria. This was done “without asking at My mouth” — they did not consult the prophet Isaiah. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- “The strength of Pharaoh” is literally “the fortress of Pharaoh,” a symbol for his kingdom. “Shadow of Egypt” is a metaphor for protection. The Cambridge Bible renders the clause “to take refuge in the refuge of Pharaoh, and to hide in the shadow of Egypt,” highlighting the irony that Egypt’s “shadow” would provide no real shelter. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Historical context:** This Pharaoh was likely So/Sevechus/Sethon (2 Kings 17:4). The setting is the Assyrian crisis under Hezekiah. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 3: *“But Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame, and the refuge of Egypt’s shade your disgrace.”*

- The very strength they trusted in would become their shame and confusion. Guzik remarks that from heaven’s perspective, “the strength of Pharaoh was nothing” — Egypt was “no substance, just a shadow.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The Gill and Ellicott commentaries agree: they would be “disappointed of the help and assistance they expected.” All who trust in an arm of flesh are sooner or later ashamed; those who trust in the Lord are never ashamed. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 4: *“For though their princes are at Zoan and their envoys have arrived in Hanes…”*

- **Zoan** = Tanis in the Nile Delta (a very old Egyptian city, once the seat of Pharaohs). **Hanes** = Heracleopolis Magna, further south. These two cities mark the extreme limits of Lower Egypt. The embassy visited all the petty courts of the Delta. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Disputed point:** Are “his princes” and “his ambassadors” those of Judah or of Pharaoh? The Cambridge Bible argues that the “his” refers to Pharaoh — the sense being, “Great as the extent of Pharaoh’s sphere of influence may be, yet nothing but shame will come to those who trust in his help.” Others take it as Judah’s princes going to Egypt. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 5: *“…everyone will be put to shame because of a people useless to them. They cannot be of help; they are good for nothing but shame and reproach.”*

- The embassy finds Egypt weak and false, without the will or power to help. Ellicott cites the Rabshakeh’s taunt (Isaiah 36) comparing Egypt to a “broken reed” that pierces the hand of anyone leaning on it, and notes that the Assyrian king Sargon boasted that Pharaoh “could not help” those who sought his alliance. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the Hebrew consonantal text (Kethib) has a harsher word — “become stinking” — while the Masoretic reading (Qere) has “come to shame.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 6: *“This is the burden against the beasts of the Negev: Through a land of hardship and distress, of lioness and lion, of viper and flying serpent, they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys… to a people of no profit to them.”*

- **The heading:** “Burden against the beasts of the Negev” is probably an ironic oracle title — the beasts of burden (donkeys and camels) carrying Judah’s treasure through the southern desert to Egypt. The “Negev” is the arid southern region of Judah. Guzik calls it “a burden against the pack animals of Judah, which would carry the riches… in a foolish attempt to purchase protection.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The “land of hardship and distress” refers to the desert wilderness, inhabited by lions, vipers, and “fiery flying serpents” (venomous serpents, cf. Numbers 21:6). Some commentators think these creatures also symbolise the dangerous character of the Egyptians themselves. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- The picture is one of pathos and irony: a caravan loaded with riches painfully crossing a dangerous desert, all to reach a nation that cannot help them. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 7: *“Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still.”*

- **“Rahab”** is a poetic name for Egypt. It means “pride” or “arrogance” and was also the name of a mythological sea-monster (cf. Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 87:4; Job 26:12). Isaiah coins the satirical nickname **“Rahab-Hem-Shebeth”** — “Rahab Sits Idle” or “Rahab the Do-Nothing.” Egypt, the boastful monster, is actually just sitting still, powerless. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- Ellicott calls this “one of those mots which stamp themselves upon a nation’s memory” — Isaiah’s political caricature. The Cambridge Bible notes that the Hebrew is obscure but the general sense is clear: “This proud boastful monster — its proper name is ‘Inaction.’” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik adds Motyer’s observation: “It is all useless, bringing neither help nor advantage… from the feared killer (Assyria) they were seeking help from the proved killer (Egypt)!” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 8: *“Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll; it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever.”*

- God commands Isaiah to document this prophecy publicly, so that when events unfold exactly as spoken, Judah will recognise that God had spoken in advance. The “tablet” suggests a public inscription; the “scroll” suggests a permanent record for later generations. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The Cambridge Bible thinks Isaiah at this time wrote a summary of all his deliverances on the Egyptian alliance, which may have become the basis for the present collection in chapters 28–32. The direction to “go in” suggests retirement to his house to prepare the record. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Gill notes that what was to be written were their sins (rebellion, trust in the arm of flesh, contempt of God’s word) and/or the prophecy of destruction, to remain “for a witness” against them. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 9: *“These are rebellious people, deceitful children, children unwilling to obey the LORD’s instruction.”*

- The written record documents the people’s character: rebellious (against God their Father), “lying children” or “faithless sons,” unwilling to hear “the law of the LORD” (the instruction given through prophets). (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- The phrase “lying children” in Hebrew can mean “false spurious ones” — they only claimed to be God’s children but did not act like it. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 10: *“They say to the seers, ‘Stop seeing visions!’ and to the prophets, ‘Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.’”*

- The people did not want to hear “right things” (things agreeable to God’s will). They demanded “smooth things” — messages of peace and prosperity despite their sinful course. This was, in effect, to demand that prophets become false prophets. Guzik notes that Paul describes the same heart in 2 Timothy 4:3-4. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The Cambridge Bible clarifies that the prophets referred to here are not merely false prophets but all representatives of the prophetic office — the people wanted even true prophets to stop speaking truth. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 11: *“Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!”*

- The people wanted the prophets to abandon their hackneyed message and stop obstructing the people’s chosen path. “Cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us” means they could not bear Isaiah’s repeated use of this divine name because it confronted them with infinite holiness. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik: “They wanted religion, but they didn’t want the living God of heaven to have a real presence in their lives.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 12: *“Therefore this is what the Holy One of Israel says: ‘Because you have rejected this message, trusting in oppression and relying on deceit…’”*

- Isaiah pointedly uses the very title the people wanted silenced — “the Holy One of Israel.” The “word” they despised was Isaiah’s message against the Egyptian alliance. “Oppression and perverseness” (or “crookedness”) probably refers to the oppressive war-taxation and crooked diplomacy of their policy. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 13: *“…this iniquity of yours is like a breach about to fail, a bulge in a high wall, whose collapse will come suddenly — in an instant!”*

- A powerful simile: a wall that bulges outward — first the threatening bulge, then the crack, then the crash — all comes “suddenly, in an instant.” The Cambridge Bible calls this a “magnificent simile” expressing how slight beginnings of transgression inevitably gravitate toward a sudden catastrophe. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- Their high towering confidence in Egypt would fall with its own weight, and they would be broken in a moment. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 14: *“It will break in pieces like a potter’s jar, shattered so that no fragment can be found… Not a shard… large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth or to skim the water from a cistern.”*

- The image of total destruction: the potter’s vessel is shattered (as in Psalm 2:9) — not merely crushed but pulverised, so completely that not even a fragment remains usable for the humblest task (scooping coals or water). This denotes “utter and irreparable ruin.” (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible notes that this shattering represents how “completely the Jewish state would be shattered by the crooked policy of its leaders.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 15: *“For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: ‘By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence — but you were not willing.’”*

- **The classic text of Isaiah’s statesmanship.** The true policy was: **returning** (turning from trust in Egypt back to God) and **rest** (ceasing from restless diplomatic striving); **quietness** (calmness before God and men) and **confidence** (trust in God’s promise). Together these would have brought salvation and strength. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Calvin (Reformed/CCEL):** He renders *shubah* as “rest” rather than “repentance,” and emphasises that the prophet “intended frequently to impress upon the people, that the Lord demands more from them than to rely fully upon him.” Calvin says the command (“be quiet”) and the promise (“you shall be saved”) are inseparable — unbelief produces uneasiness; faith brings calm. (CCEL/Calvin: https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom14/calcom14.xix.i.html)
- **MacLaren (Baptist/evangelical):** He observes that the two clauses of v. 15 are in inverted parallelism: “returning and rest” correspond to “quietness and confidence.” “Returning” means “just to trust” — we come back to God not by preparing ourselves or by our own expiation, but by simple confidence. The ground of this confidence is our knowledge of God, especially in Jesus Christ. (MacLaren, via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/maclaren/isa_jer.ii.i.xxx.html)
- **Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist):** In commenting on the related verses, Spurgeon calls quietness and confidence “the still small voice” that brings the soul back to communion with God. On v. 15 he writes: “It is always weakness to be fretting and worrying, questioning and mistrusting… We are sinking by our struggles when we might float by faith.” (Spurgeon, via Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-devotionals-c-h-spurgeon)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (Reformed/evangelical):** “Returning and rest” means turning back from the Egyptian embassy and ceasing warlike preparations; “quietness” answers to “wait for Him” (v. 18). (JFB, via CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb/jfb.x.xxiii.xxxi.html)
- **Gill (Reformed Baptist)** extends the application to spiritual salvation: repentance is “returning,” faith is “rest” and “confidence” — going to Christ alone for rest, placing confidence in Him and deriving peace from Him alone. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Summarises four aspects of trusting God’s promise: returning, rest, quietness, and confidence. “There is no person walking this earth more powerful than a child of God boldly and properly trusting the promise of the living God.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The final clause “but you were not willing” is a devastating statement: they had the offer but refused it. Their will was the obstacle.

### v. 16: *“‘No,’ you say, ‘we will flee on horses.’ Therefore you will flee! ‘We will ride swift horses,’ but your pursuers will be faster.”*

- There is a wordplay in Hebrew between “horses” (*susim*) and “flee/swift.” The horses they boasted in (expected as Egypt’s military contribution) would only be useful for a more rapid retreat, not for the charge of battle. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik: “Because Judah rejected God’s promise, and trusted in horses and other such things instead, they would need to flee! If they would have trusted God’s promise instead, they would never have had reason to flee.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 17: *“A thousand will flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you will all flee, until you are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill.”*

- This is a reversal of the covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:8 (“five shall chase a hundred”) and a fulfilment of the curse of Leviticus 26:17 (“you shall flee when no one pursues you”). Instead of Israel routing enemies, the enemy puts them to flight. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The imagery of a solitary “pole” (or pine tree) on a mountaintop and a “banner” (flag-staff) on a hill paints a picture of utter isolation and desolation — a remnant left standing alone. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 18: *“Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God. Blessed are all who wait for Him.”*

- **The great turning point of the chapter.** After the grim judgment, verse 18 opens a new section full of glorious promises. “Therefore” may have adversative force — “nevertheless, even under these circumstances.” The Lord’s “waiting” is one of eager, anxious expectancy for the opportune moment to intervene. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik: “Whenever the LORD waits or seems to delay, it always has a loving purpose behind it.” God can be both just and merciful simultaneously — most fully demonstrated at the cross, where Jesus took the punishment we deserve (justice) and God extends that work to us (mercy). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- **Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist)** preached a full sermon on this verse (“A Waiting God and a Waiting People”). He describes the people as “in a great hurry to be delivered” — they could not wait God’s time but wanted instant rescue. He warns believers against the same fault: “If in poverty, they are in haste to be rich; and they shall not long be innocent. If under reproach, their heart ferments towards revenge.” The holy art is to learn to wait. (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-waiting-god-and-a-waiting-people)
- Ellicott: “Man’s extremity is God’s opportunity.” The Lord “was waiting, i.e., longing, with an eager expectation, to come to the rescue.” (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 19: *“O people in Zion who dwell in Jerusalem, you will weep no more. He will surely be gracious when you cry for help; when He hears, He will answer you.”*

- The promise is addressed to “people in Zion,” the faithful remnant. “You shall weep no more… He will be very gracious to you at the sound of your cry.” Even if God feels distant, He hears and promises to answer. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- The Cambridge Bible: The answer to prayer is immediate — “weep thou shalt not, he will surely be gracious.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 20: *“The Lord will give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, but your Teacher will no longer hide Himself — with your own eyes you will see Him.”*

- “Bread of adversity” and “water of affliction” refer to meagre rations — the scant fare of a siege (cf. 1 Kings 22:27). The Cambridge Bible connects this to the period of distress preceding the great deliverance. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Key textual question: “Teacher” (singular) or “teachers” (plural)?** The Hebrew verb is singular. The Cambridge Bible argues it means God Himself as the personal Teacher of His people — a striking Messianic concept: “thy Teacher (God) hide Himself no more.” The alternative rendering “teachers” would refer to the prophets who are now driven into concealment but will then appear publicly. The Cambridge Bible favours God as Teacher because the concept fits the Messianic age and the next verse speaks of a voice “behind you.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik, taking “teachers” (plural): “When Judah was prosperous and comfortable, they wouldn’t listen to God. Now, God gave them the bread of adversity and water of affliction, but they could hear God and be guided by Him again.” Adversity opened their ears. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- Ellicott notes that in the mission of Isaiah 37:2 (when Hezekiah sent to Isaiah during the Assyrian crisis) there was a virtual fulfilment of this prediction — the true teachers were at last recognised. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 21: *“And whether you turn to the right or to the left, your ears will hear this command behind you: ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’”*

- The voice “behind you” is that of the Teacher — like a Father walking behind His children, directing their steps. It is an inner voice that echoes and confirms the voice of the human teacher. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- **Spurgeon** preached an entire sermon on this verse (“The Voice Behind Thee”). He described it as “the still small voice” that reaches both the ear and the heart, warning and teaching, guiding the believer at every turn. He connected it to the guidance of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament era. (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-voice-behind-thee)

### v. 22: *“So you will desecrate your silver-plated idols and your gold-plated images. You will throw them away like menstrual cloths, saying to them, ‘Be gone!’”*

- The first effect of the people’s turning to God will be the putting away of their besetting sin — idolatry. The “graven images” were carved wooden figures overlaid with silver and gold. These would be desecrated and thrown away like something loathsome. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik notes that the Hebrew word translated “unclean thing” in some versions is literally “a menstrual cloth” (so KJV and NIV). The point: God’s people would come to hate their idols so much they would throw them away as readily as a used menstrual cloth. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 23: *“Then He will send rain for the seed that you have sown in the ground, and the food that comes from your land will be rich and plentiful. On that day your cattle will graze in open pastures.”*

- Following repentance and the renunciation of idols, God promises outward material blessings. The “rain of thy seed” is the early rain falling in October. The bread will be “fat and plentiful,” and cattle will feed in large pastures. The Cambridge Bible notes that Isaiah follows Joel (Joel 2:21-26) in picturing outward plenty following the renewal of inner life. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 24: *“The oxen and donkeys that work the ground will eat salted fodder, winnowed with shovel and pitchfork.”*

- **“Salted fodder”** (or “clean provender”) was a luxury — corn mixed with salt or alkaline herbs, made from the finest winnowed grain. In normal times, cattle ate inferior barley mixed with chopped straw. That even the lowly donkeys would eat this choice feed marks “the ne plus ultra of plenty.” (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible cites an Arabic proverb: “Sweet fodder is the camel’s bread; salted fodder is his comfit.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 25: *“And from every high mountain and every raised hill, streams of water will flow in the day of great slaughter, when the towers fall.”*

- Even the arid hilltops of Palestine will flow with rivers. This coincides with “the day of great slaughter” — a day of judgment on the enemies of God’s people (perhaps the Assyrian host) and/or the fall of towers in which they trusted. The Cambridge Bible calls this “a vague poetic allusion to the day of the LORD, when all His enemies are destroyed.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik connects the “great slaughter” to the angel of the LORD killing 185,000 Assyrians (2 Kings 19:35). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 26: *“The light of the moon will be as bright as the sun, and the light of the sun will be seven times brighter — like the light of seven days — on the day that the LORD binds up the brokenness of His people and heals the wounds He has inflicted.”*

- The vision expands from the new earth to the new heaven — a transformed creation where sun and moon shine with supernatural brightness. Light is the symbol of divine glory. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- “Sevenfold… as the light of seven days” means the light of an entire week concentrated into one day. The Cambridge Bible notes this clause is absent from the Septuagint and may be a late gloss. (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- The healing language — “bind up the breach… heal the stroke of their wound” — echoes Isaiah 1:6. Better than material blessing is God’s loving care. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- **Different readings of eschatology:** Some (Guzik) see this as fulfilled partially in the Assyrian deliverance and fully in the Messianic age; others see it as purely eschatological. The traditional Christian reading across traditions sees it as pointing to the new creation in the Messianic kingdom.

### v. 27: *“Behold, the Name of the LORD comes from afar, with burning anger and dense smoke. His lips are full of fury, and His tongue is like a consuming fire.”*

- **“The Name of the LORD”** is a striking expression, almost a personification — parallel to “the glory of Jehovah.” Ellicott notes it as “an anticipation of the later use of the *memra* (Word) in the Targumim, and of the *logos* of St. John, a distinct, though not defined, conception of a duality in the Divine essence.” (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- The imagery is of a theophany — God appearing like a thunderstorm on the distant horizon, with thick uplifting smoke and fire. The Cambridge Bible: “Jehovah’s coming is like that of the thundercloud which appears on the distant horizon, no eye having observed the mysterious process by which it was formed.” (Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 28: *“His breath is like a rushing torrent that rises to the neck. He comes to sift the nations in a sieve of destruction; He bridles the jaws of the peoples to lead them astray.”*

- Water and fire symbolism combine. God’s breath (wrath) is an overflowing torrent that reaches the neck — threatening to engulf all in its path. He “sifts the nations with the sieve of vanity” — winnows them until they are annihilated. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- The “bridle in the jaws” echoes Isaiah 37:29 — God leads enemies against their will to their own destruction. Ellicott quotes the Latin: *Quem Deus vult perdere, prius dementat* (“Whom God wishes to destroy, he first makes mad”). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 29: *“You will sing as on the night of a holy festival, and your heart will rejoice like one who walks to the music of a flute, going up to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel.”*

- While judgment falls on the nations, God’s people sing. The “holy festival” is likely the Passover (the only feast with a distinct night ritual) or the Feast of Tabernacles, which was the most joyous of all festivals. The second clause pictures the day-ritual: pilgrims processing with flutes, bringing firstfruits to the Temple. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Cambridge: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm)
- “Rock of Israel” (*tsur*) is a name of Jehovah (cf. Deuteronomy 32:4). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik: “Boldness and joy in the day of judgment are precious gifts from God… God’s people are here portrayed rejoicing at His judgment on sin because they must take His point of view on everything, and because this judgment is at the same time their salvation.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 30: *“And the LORD will cause His majestic voice to be heard and His mighty arm to be revealed, striking in angry wrath with a flame of consuming fire, and with cloudburst, storm, and hailstones.”*

- The theophany intensifies. God’s “glorious voice” is thunder; the “lighting down of His arm” is His descending stroke of power. “Hailstones and coals of fire” are natural symbols of divine wrath. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- Guzik wants readers to see “the glory of God’s judgments. When we understand how God’s perfect judgment exalts His justice and His righteousness, we see the glory of the judgment of the LORD.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 31: *“For Assyria will be shattered at the voice of the LORD; He will strike them with His scepter.”*

- Assyria is named as the foremost enemy. The prediction points specifically to the destruction of Sennacherib’s armies (Isaiah 37:36). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

### v. 32: *“And with every stroke of the rod of punishment that the LORD brings down on them, the tambourines and lyres will sound as He battles with weapons brandished.”*

- At every stroke of God’s judgments upon Assyria, Israel would raise songs of triumph with tambourines (timbrels) and harps (or lutes) — as after Jephthah’s and David’s victories (Judges 11:34; 1 Samuel 18:6). Ellicott likens it to singing a *Te Deum* over the fall of the enemy. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- “Battles of shaking” (or “swinging”) describes the action of a warrior swinging his sword rapidly to and fro, striking enemies at every stroke. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)

### v. 33: *“For Topheth has long been prepared; it has been made ready for the king. Its funeral pyre is deep and wide, with plenty of fire and wood. The breath of the LORD, like a torrent of burning sulfur, sets it ablaze.”*

- **Tophet** (or Topheth) was a place in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where Ahaz and others had sacrificed children to Molech (2 Kings 16:3; Jeremiah 7:31). The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom → Gehenna) became Jerusalem’s rubbish dump with smouldering fires — a picture of hell. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- **“For the king”** — the king of Assyria (Sennacherib). Ellicott notes a grim wordplay: “for the melek” (the king) echoes “Molech” — the Assyrian king would become a sacrifice to the very god whose cult was practised in that valley. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm)
- The pyre is “deep and wide” with abundant fire and wood, kindled by the breath of the LORD like a stream of brimstone. Guzik: “God had a special place in hell for the Assyrian king… though he did not die at Jerusalem” — historically, his own sons murdered him in the temple of Nisroch (2 Kings 19:36-37). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)
- Trapp (Puritan, cited by Guzik): “Great men, if not good, shall be greatly tormented; and the more they have of the fat of the earth, the more they are sure to fry in hell.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/)

## TRADITIONAL READINGS: WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS DIFFER

### v. 15 — The Nature of “Returning and Rest”

- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin emphasises that the command and promise are inseparable; unbelief alone produces uneasiness. The “returning” is primarily turning from human trust to divine trust — less about ritual repentance, more about a fundamental reorientation of confidence. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom14/calcom14.xix.i.html
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, MacLaren):** MacLaren defines “returning” as simply trusting God — “we come back to God by simple confidence, not by preparing ourselves, not by our expiation, but only by trusting in Him.” This expresses a classic evangelical/Baptist emphasis on faith alone. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/maclaren/isa_jer.ii.i.xxx.html
- **Reformed Baptist (Gill):** Gill spiritualises the verse fully: “repentance may be meant by ‘returning,’ and faith by ‘rest’; or by ‘returning and rest’ may be designed returning to rest, that is, to Christ, who is the only rest to weary souls.” This merges a Puritan/Covenant theology with the gospel call. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/30.htm
- **Pentecostal/charismatic (Guzik):** Emphasises the active/practical dimensions: returning means drawing close to the Lord and turning from disobedience; rest means ceasing from frantic self-protection; quietness means not arguing for one’s own side; confidence means freedom from despair. The stress is on the believer’s posture of active trust. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/

### v. 20 — “Teacher” or “Teachers”?

- **Cambridge Bible** argues for the singular “Teacher” = God Himself, as the personal instructor of His people in the Messianic age. This reading has some Reformed support as pointing to divine illumination. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm
- **Guzik (Pentecostal)** and **Ellicott (Anglican)** take the plural “teachers,” referring to the prophets who are no longer hidden but publicly recognised. This reading sees the restoration of faithful human ministry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm
- There is no strong denominational divide here; it is a textual decision. Both readings are found across traditions.

### v. 26 — Eschatological Reading

- The supernatural transformation of sun and moon is generally read across all Protestant traditions as pointing forward to the new creation and the Messianic age. The Cambridge Bible places it in the context of Isaiah’s vision of a transformed “new heaven and new earth.” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm
- Guzik sees both a near-term fulfilment (the blessings after Assyria’s defeat) and an ultimate eschatological fulfilment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/

### v. 33 — Tophet and Hell

- The traditional reading across nearly all Protestant traditions (Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal, Anglican) is that Tophet = the Valley of Hinnom = Gehenna = a type of hell. The Assyrian king’s destined fate in Tophet prefigures the final judgment of the wicked.
- Ellicott adds the historical note that the corpses of the Assyrian dead after the angelic slaughter were probably literally burned in the Valley of Hinnom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/30.htm
- Guzik (Pentecostal) and Trapp (Puritan) emphasise the eternal dimension: the king of Assyria was “reserved for hell itself.” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-30/

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

Unfortunately, I could not reach newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search and fetch limits available. No Catholic or Orthodox-specific commentary on Isaiah 30 was retrieved.

### Modern Scholarship

- The **NET Bible** notes could not be individually fetched, but the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges (late 19th/early 20th century critical scholarship) represents a moderate critical approach. It notes textual issues (e.g., the “beasts of the south” heading may be an editorial gloss; the “light of seven days” clause in v. 26 is absent from the LXX and may be a later addition). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm
- On v. 4–5, the Cambridge Bible notes that Lower Egypt was ruled at this time by “a number of petty potentates,” with the prince of Sais holding primacy — reflecting the historical situation of the 25th Dynasty period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/30.htm

### Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace Readings

No specific results from these movements were found for Isaiah 30 within the available sources. Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic tradition) applies v. 23–26 to material blessing following repentance but within the framework of covenant faithfulness, not a mechanistic prosperity formula.
